content: I'm involved in debugging the nightly-testing branch of cslib. Recently something happened to grind that broke many previously working grind proofs. It is extremely painful to try to figure out what's going on. I tried to use grind? in the old working branch to obtain the lemmas that grind used in a successful proof and port them to the new failing branch. That did not work. In one case the new grind is not able to find a certain definition which, once given to grind, finishes the proof successfully. But that definition did not appear in the list of lemmas returned by grind? in the old branch. What I would like to have is the following feature: a option to make grind output a proof that is guaranteed to work in the future. This proof can be grind-free or invokes a base layer of grind that is guaranteed to stay stable. It is OK if this proof is very large. All we need is some hints that can help a poor human to figure out how to fix a proof. Is this possible?

Some additional context for those that may not use grind as much. If there is any breakage of a proof across toolchains, usually one of the helpful things to do is use grind? to see what theorems and local hypothesis (appearing as hash codes) are used. But we have observed that sometimes the behavior of grind? (on a successful grind proof) can be a bit unexpected. It can fail to produce a grind only or interactive mode script that is able to close the given goal, omitting theorems and producing invalid hashes. So in a situation where you're debugging a broken proof, you're essentially left to reprove the theorem or intuit the grind changes.

With this knowledge, I've now started checking for this while reviewing PRs for Mathlib and CSLib, as this seems like a maintainability issue that may be difficult to detect until much later when it arises unexpectedly. While this is out of my scope to address more systemically, I have started work on a tactic analysis linter to detect when a theorem uses grind that does not have any valid output from grind?. This may not be perfect, as these usually run in periodic reports, but I think is a good start in identifying these cases.

Re-proving a theorem can be very painful even for the person who came up with the original proof. It would be even worse if that person is no longer around. If we want grind to be widely used, the maintainability of proofs using grind is a very important desideratum.

We've made a big change to grind in lean#13166, which has landed in v4.30.0-rc1, which is both significantly more performant, but also much less willing to make use of defeq abuses. It is disruptive, and we're thinking about it, but ... patience is much appreciated as we make these changes. :-) I think so far most of the problems we've seen with grind in v4.30 are actually attributable to defeq abuses in libraries that grind was previously willing to make use of.

But minimizations of problems are very helpful.

Similarly, minimizations of cases where grind? suggests incorrect proofs are also useful.
The basic architecture of grind makes it impossible for grind to generate entirely grind free proofs. There's simply too much infrastructure.

I agree that the particular changes about defeq abuse are probably good, and am happy to be patient here.

I'd like to help by reporting grind? minimizations, but have been putting it off because it seemed pretty painstaking. Is this sort of failure in scope for your lean-minimizer? I wasn't sure if it would pick up everything a call to grind depends on.

Kim Morrison said:

I think so far most of the problems we've seen with grind in v4.30 are actually attributable to defeq abuses in libraries that grind was previously willing to make use of.

Is Mathlib one of the "libraries", and this impacts downstream projects? I understand there must be technical difficulties in this and I am patient, but looking at this from a different perspective, it sounds like Lean is holding downstream project owner hostage to force certain large scale change in Mathlib. I hope that's not the actual case, but this is the second time it gives me the feeling (last time it was defeq.respectTransparency)
How are you held hostage when nobody forces you to update to newer versions of Lean?

There are at least two forces:

  1. one might want new features from the new version of Lean. Otherwise, why is Lean updating at all?
  2. New projects are automatically created on the latest version
in a strict sense, indeed no one is forcing you to update, but it is more like "ask mathlib to fix their thing if you want to enjoy better Lean"
I mean, that can be an ok workflow if everything is communicated transparently and everyone is prepared

For big changes in the future, would it be possible to provide a per-invocation option that restores the old behavior, so that people can use it to get more time to fix the problems after updating to a new version? In the case of cslib, we have been extremely lucky to have Chris fixing most the problems in a short period of time, while he’s traveling. We may not be so lucky in the future.

I consider keeping mathlib up to date with recent Lean to be part of all maintainers' job (and us to be very lucky that Kim and others at the FRO are helping so much). That is not a license to make any change, but I trust the FRO to keep current users in mind.
It would indeed be great to have more support and funding for cslib maintenance (but I'm not aware of any hair on fire problems).

I have not felt an undue burden from maintaining such changes, especially considering the relative scales of CSLib and Mathlib. If this changes, I will be sure to make it known. I agree with Michael that it is a responsibility that I have happily chosen to take on for CSLib, especially considering that I have been a big proponent of experimenting with using grind (sometimes in excess). In particular, I think this change is a principled one that prompts us to address existing defeq abuse issues.
Indeed, backward compatibility switches have been provided in the past. (Doing so for every change also comes at a cost to core Lean, so this is a trade-off!)

Chris Henson said:

I have started work on a tactic analysis linter...

I have just opened #37916 for this, which was made much simpler by some work that Kim had already done. I currently count 117 places in Mathlib where grind? will produce an invalid grind only. Spot checking some of these, I notice a couple of patterns:

  • certain modifiers like cases seem to fail to appear in the suggestions
  • lots of failures are omitting theorems about Set, maybe related to the defeq abuse changes?
Thank you, @Chris Henson, this is super helpful. I hope that we can next use the https://github.com/leanprover-community/minimize tool to get some of these examples minimized and then fixed!
